tip: The sound of a video: voices, music and noises.
meaning: Audio is everything you hear. People forgive a slightly bad picture, but not bad sound, so audio matters a lot.
example: A great shot with a crackling voice is hard to watch.
vukem: Sound lives on audio tracks. See [Audio](/docs/guide/audio).

tip: The picture of a sound: tall where it is loud, flat where it is quiet.
meaning: A waveform draws the loudness of a sound over time. It lets you see the beats of a song or the silences in a talk.
example: A clap shows as a tall spike on the waveform.

tip: How loud a sound is.
meaning: Volume is how strong a sound is. Turning it up makes the sound louder, turning it down makes it quieter.
example: Lower the music so you can hear the talking.
vukem: An item has a `volume` from 0 to 4 (a multiplier). 1 is the original. See [Audio](/docs/guide/audio).

tip: The unit used to measure how strong or loud a sound is, written dB.
meaning: Decibels measure loudness on a scale that matches how ears hear: a small number change can be a big difference in how loud it seems. Adding 6 dB roughly doubles the strength of a signal.
example: A whisper is about 30 dB and a rock concert about 110 dB.

tip: How loud a sound feels to a person over time, not just its highest bump.
meaning: A short loud bang and a long steady hum can have the same highest point, but the hum feels louder. Loudness measures how loud it feels.
example: Two songs that peak the same can still be one louder than the other.
vukem: The project has a `loudness_target` (LUFS) that the export aims for.

tip: The standard unit for how loud a whole video sounds, like -14 LUFS.
meaning: LUFS measures loudness the way ears do, averaged over the whole video. Websites and TV have a target number and make loud videos quieter.
example: A platform that wants about -14 LUFS turns a -8 LUFS video down.

tip: The highest point a sound reaches.
meaning: The peak is the loudest instant. If it is too high, the sound distorts.
example: A balloon pop is a tall, short peak.

tip: Distortion that happens when a sound is too loud for the system.
meaning: When a sound goes above the highest level, the top of the wave is chopped flat and it crackles. Once it is clipped you cannot fix it, so avoid it when recording.
example: A shout into a phone microphone sounds ugly and broken.

tip: The safety space between your loudest point and the limit.
meaning: Headroom is how much louder the sound could get before it breaks. Leaving some prevents clipping.
example: Recording a voice at a middle level leaves room if the person suddenly laughs loudly.

tip: Raising or lowering a whole sound so it reaches a chosen level.
meaning: Normalizing changes the volume of the whole file by one amount, so the loudest point or the average loudness hits a target.
example: Make a very quiet voice recording as loud as the others.

tip: A tool that makes loud parts quieter, so the volume is more even.
meaning: A compressor squeezes the difference between loud and quiet. Voices become easier to understand, because the whispers and the shouts are closer together.
example: A narrator who whispers and then shouts sounds steady after compression.

tip: A tool that stops a sound from going above a chosen level.
meaning: A limiter is a very strict compressor: the sound simply cannot pass the limit, so it cannot clip.
example: A safety net placed at the end of the sound chain.

tip: A tool that makes high, middle or low sounds louder or quieter.
meaning: An equalizer works like the bass and treble knobs on a speaker. Cut the low rumble from a voice or boost the highs to make it clearer.
example: Remove the wind rumble from an outdoor interview.

tip: Removing a hiss, hum or background noise from a recording.
meaning: Software can learn what the noise sounds like and take it out. Too much makes voices sound robotic.
example: Taking the fridge hum out of a kitchen interview.

tip: The quiet sound of a place when nobody is talking.
meaning: Every room has its own faint sound. Recording a bit of it lets editors fill silent gaps so the sound does not suddenly go dead.
example: Filming 30 seconds of the classroom being quiet.

tip: The background sounds of a place, like wind, traffic or a crowd.
meaning: Ambience tells the viewer where they are. A forest has birds, a street has cars.
example: Adding the sound of waves to a beach video recorded in a quiet room.

tip: A short sound added to match something on screen, like a pop or a whoosh.
meaning: Sound effects make actions feel real or funny. A door slam, a click, a swoosh when a title slides in.
example: A whoosh when a text slides on screen.

tip: Everyday sounds recorded on purpose to match the action in a film.
meaning: Foley artists make small sounds by hand, like footsteps, rustling clothes or cracking celery for breaking bones.
example: Walking on gravel in a studio to make the sound of someone walking in a movie.

tip: A voice you hear, but the speaker is not shown speaking.
meaning: A voice-over is a narrator talking over the pictures, explaining or telling the story.
example: A nature video where someone tells you about the lion we see.

tip: The words people say to each other in a video.
meaning: Dialogue is spoken conversation. It carries the story, so it needs to be clear above everything else.
example: Two friends talking in a scene.

tip: Quiet background music under talking or pictures.
meaning: A music bed supports a scene without taking attention from the voice. It is usually kept much lower than the speaker.
example: Soft piano under a story told by a narrator.

tip: The music written for a film or video.
meaning: A score is music made to match a story, with moods that change with the scenes.
example: The scary music that starts before the monster appears.

tip: Making music automatically quieter while someone is talking.
meaning: Ducking lowers the music when a voice speaks and lets it come back after, so you can always hear the words.
example: Radio presenters do it: the song gets quieter when they speak.
vukem: `audio.duck` lowers a music item under speech. See [Audio](/docs/guide/audio).

tip: Balancing all the sounds of a video so each is heard at the right level.
meaning: Mixing sets the loudness of voice, music and effects relative to each other, so nothing hides something else.
example: Voice in front, music behind, a small whoosh on top.
vukem: An export mixes every audio track together.

tip: A group of sounds mixed together, like all the music or all the voices.
meaning: A stem is one part of the mix saved on its own. Because they are separate, another version, like another language, can be made easily.
example: A file with only the music and another with only the voices.

tip: Sound on one channel, the same in every speaker.
meaning: Mono sound is a single channel. It does not have left and right. Many microphones record mono.
example: A voice recorded with one microphone.

tip: Sound on two channels, left and right, so things can be placed on either side.
meaning: Stereo has a left and a right speaker, which gives a sense of space. A car can drive from the left to the right.
example: Wearing headphones, a bee flies from your left ear to your right.
vukem: A WAV export is 16-bit, 48 kHz stereo.

tip: Sound from many speakers around you, like 5.1 in a cinema.
meaning: Surround adds speakers behind and beside you so sounds can come from all around. 5.1 means five speakers and one for deep bass.
example: A helicopter that seems to fly over your head in a cinema.

tip: How many times per second the sound is measured when it is stored.
meaning: Digital sound is a list of measurements. The sample rate says how many are taken per second. Video usually uses 48,000 (48 kHz).
example: A music CD uses 44,100 samples per second; video uses 48,000.

tip: How finely each sound measurement is written down.
meaning: More bits mean finer steps between quiet and loud, and less noise in quiet parts. 16 bits is common, 24 bits is used for recording.
example: A 24-bit recording keeps the quiet details better than 8 bits.

tip: The steady pulse of music that you can tap your foot to.
meaning: The beat is the regular pulse in a song. Cutting your video on the beat makes it feel good.
example: Clap along to a song: each clap is a beat.
vukem: `audio.mark_beats` writes a marker on each beat. See [Audio](/docs/guide/audio).

tip: Beats per minute: how fast a song is.
meaning: BPM counts the beats in one minute. 60 BPM is one beat each second. 120 BPM is two beats each second.
example: A slow ballad may be 70 BPM and a dance track 128 BPM.

tip: Sound and mouth movement that match in time.
meaning: When the picture and the sound are even slightly out of time, a talking person looks wrong. Fixing that is called sync.
example: You hear "hello" a moment after you see the lips close.

tip: The echo-like tail of a sound in a big space, like a church.
meaning: Reverb is many little echoes that melt together. A bathroom and a big hall each have their own reverb.
example: Clapping in an empty gym: the clap keeps ringing.

tip: How high or low a sound is.
meaning: A mouse squeak is high-pitched and a lion roar is low-pitched. Changing the pitch makes a voice higher or lower without changing the speed.
example: A chipmunk voice is a voice with the pitch raised.

tip: Choosing how much of a sound goes left and how much goes right.
meaning: Panning places a sound between the left and the right speaker, so it seems to come from a place.
example: A bird chirping from the left side of the picture.
